university: University of California, San Diego (UC San Diego)

program_meta.program_name: PhD in Computer Science (or Computer Engineering), Department of Computer Science & Engineering (CSE), Jacobs School of Engineering. faculty.department: Electrical & Computer Engineering (primary); Associate Adjunct Professor, Division of Biomedical Informatics, Dept. of Medicine; Affiliated Faculty, HDSI, AI Group in CSE, Bioengineering, Institute of Engineering in Medicine
faculty.lab: Pengtao Xie Lab / UCSD ML for Healthcare and Biology group
faculty.research_areas: Label-efficient and sample-efficient medical image segmentation; generative-model-based data augmentation for ultra-low-data regimes; self-supervised and curriculum pretraining; multi-level / bi-level optimisation for training-data and pretraining-objective design; foundation models and LLM agents for healthcare and biology; neural architecture search.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's A-PDF work generates synthetic MRI with a conditional WGAN-GP and then FILTERS the generated images with a Mahalanobis / kNN score against the class-proportion distribution of 447 real masks (retaining only 33.7% / 35.1%) instead of trusting the discriminator - i.e. quality control on synthetic training data. Xie's 'Generative AI enables medical image segmentation in ultra low-data regimes' (GenSeg, Nature Communications 2025, selected as a Nature Communications Editors' Highlight) is the same problem attacked from the other end: an end-to-end generative pipeline that makes segmentation work when annotations are nearly absent. Xie also published 'Position: Creating High-Fidelity Synthetic Training Data Should Employ Multi-level Optimization' (ICML 2026), which is a direct methodological answer to the question Akshat's post-hoc filter leaves open (filter after generation vs. optimise the generator against downstream segmentation loss). Second axis: Akshat's semi-supervised spine result (teacher 0.735 mIoU on 54 labelled images -> filtered pseudo-labels -> student 0.816 mIoU, +8.1 points) is exactly the ultra-low-data regime Xie's 'Sample Efficient Biomedical Image Semantic Segmentation' talk series is about, and 'BLO-SAM: Bi-level Optimization Based Overfitting-Preventing Finetuning of the Segment Anything Model' (ICML 2024) is the label-scarce-finetuning counterpart of Akshat's frozen-vs-finetuned DDPM encoder ablation.
faculty.key_paper_1: Li Zhang, Basu Jindal, Ahmed Alaa, Robert Weinreb, David Wilson, Eran Segal, James Zou, Pengtao Xie. 'Generative AI enables medical image segmentation in ultra low-data regimes.' Nature Communications, 2025.
faculty.key_paper_2: Li Zhang, Youwei Liang, Pengtao Xie. 'BLO-SAM: Bi-level Optimization Based Overfitting-Preventing Finetuning of the Segment Anything Model.' International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), 2024.

faculty.email_angle: Your GenSeg result - segmentation that holds up in ultra-low-data regimes - is the problem I hit from the opposite direction: I built a conditional WGAN-GP for lumbar MRI and then discarded two-thirds of its output using a Mahalanobis score on real class-proportion statistics, because the discriminator was not a reliable proxy for anatomical plausibility; I would like to ask whether that filter should instead be folded into the generator objective as your ICML 2026 position paper argues.
faculty.notes: STRONGEST MATCH AT UCSD, and the only one of the four Close matches with an unambiguous open-door contact policy that names the CSE PhD program explicitly. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: his PRIMARY appointment is ECE, not CSE - but he tells applicants to apply to CSE and he is a member of the CSE AI Group, so a CSE PhD application naming him should route correctly. Second caveat: his 2025-2026 output has drifted heavily toward LLM agents, multimodal reasoning reward models (DreamPRM), and biology foundation models (scLong, ProteinAligner); the medical-imaging-under-scarcity thread is real and recent (Nature Comms 2025) but is no longer the centre of gravity of the lab. Ask directly whether he is still taking imaging students. He also explicitly accepts master's students, which makes him the best single name for the MSCS fallback.

faculty.lab: Statistical Visual Computing Laboratory (SVCL), which he heads
faculty.research_areas: Statistical/data-efficient visual learning; taxonomic and hierarchical classification with consistency guarantees; calibration and selective prediction; long-tailed and open-set recognition; diffusion-model control and negative sampling; machine teaching and crowd annotation of expert-domain data; medical imaging collaborations (glaucoma/OCT-A with Shiley Eye Institute, cervical brachytherapy auto-planning with Radiation Oncology).
faculty.why_match: This is a near-collision with HiME. Akshat's HiME composes per-level conditional sigmoids by the chain rule so that a child's probability can never exceed its parent's, giving an upward-closed prediction set and hierarchy consistency BY CONSTRUCTION (Prop. 1, a theorem rather than a measurement) - validated on Galaxy Zoo 2, 239,573 images, 37 classes, 4 levels, 95.8% decision-level accuracy, with only ~0.01% parameter overhead across 5 backbones. Vasconcelos's 'ProTeCt: Prompt Tuning for Taxonomic Open Set Classification' (CVPR 2024, with Tz-Ying Wu and Chih-Hui Ho) attacks precisely the same failure mode - models that are accurate per level but inconsistent across a taxonomy - and does so with a lightweight prompt-tuning intervention rather than an architectural constraint. That is a direct, testable disagreement Akshat can name: prompt-level repair vs. decode-rule guarantee. His earlier 'Solving Long-tailed Recognition with Deep Realistic Taxonomic Classifier' (ECCV 2020) is the ancestor of the same line. Second axis: Akshat's spine paper swept confidence thresholding against MC-dropout uncertainty for pseudo-label filtering and found combining them adds nothing, and that thresholds calibrated on 5 reference images match those from 304 - a calibration-efficiency result. Vasconcelos's 'Towards Calibrated Multi-label Deep Neural Networks' (CVPR 2024) and 'Leveraging Data to Say No: Memory Augmented Plug-and-Play Selective Prediction' (ICLR 2026) are the principled versions of that same abstain/threshold machinery.
faculty.key_paper_1: Tz-Ying Wu*, Chih-Hui Ho*, Nuno Vasconcelos. 'ProTeCt: Prompt Tuning for Taxonomic Open Set Classification.' IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), Seattle, 2024.
faculty.key_paper_2: Jiacheng Cheng, Nuno Vasconcelos. 'Towards Calibrated Multi-label Deep Neural Networks.' IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), Seattle, 2024. (See also: Aditya Sarkar, Yi Li, Jiacheng Cheng, Shlok Mishra, Nuno Vasconcelos, 'Leveraging Data to Say No: Memory Augmented Plug-and-Play Selective Prediction,' ICLR 2026.)

faculty.email: nuno@ucsd.edu (listed on his homepage in spaced form: 'n u n o @ u c s d . e d u')
faculty.email_angle: ProTeCt repairs taxonomic inconsistency through prompt tuning; I took the opposite route and made it impossible - per-level conditional sigmoids composed by the chain rule give an upward-closed prediction set on Galaxy Zoo 2 (239,573 images, 4 levels) for ~0.01% extra parameters - and I found the constraint costs accuracy under a frozen encoder while being free under full fine-tuning, which is the tradeoff I would like your read on.
faculty.notes: The prior shortlist's flag on Vasconcelos is CONFIRMED and is if anything understated - the taxonomic-consistency overlap with HiME is tighter than 'data-efficient visual learning' suggests. BUT THE CRITICAL LOGISTICAL CATCH: he is ECE, not CSE, and his own page says admission must come through ECE and that applicants must select the 'Signal and Image Processing' area or 'the SVCL faculty will probably never see your application.' A CSE-only application will NOT reach him. If he is a serious target, Akshat must either apply to ECE (and lose the CSE application, since UCSD allows only one degree level per department but does permit separate applications to different departments - each with its own $155 fee) or accept that CSE is the wrong door for this lab. Also note SVCL's stated funding constraint, and that a large share of the lab's 2024-2026 output is now diffusion/VLM/video-reasoning and clinical collaborations (glaucoma OCT-A, cervical brachytherapy) rather than core label-efficiency. He is emphatically NOT emeritus and NOT on leave.

faculty.department: Cognitive Science, Division of Social Sciences (PRIMARY); Computer Science and Engineering (AFFILIATE)
faculty.lab: Machine Learning, Perception, and Cognition Lab (mlPC)
faculty.research_areas: Generative representation learning (diffusion models, introspective/generative-discriminative hybrids, VAEs); structured prediction and image parsing; vision transformers; multimodal LLMs; historically, weakly-supervised and semi-supervised medical image segmentation (histopathology, brain MRI, CT).
faculty.why_match: Akshat's diffusion work pretrains a DDPM on unlabelled abdominal CT and transfers the encoder to organ segmentation (liver Dice 0.751 -> 0.928; a FROZEN encoder retains 87% of the fine-tuned liver Dice, but the frozen kidney encoder FAILS, scoring below random init) - and the open question he cares about is why learned generative priors transfer for some anatomical structures and not others. Tu's 'Bayesian Diffusion Models for 3D Shape Reconstruction' (CVPR 2024) is exactly the machinery for that question: it couples a learned diffusion prior with a discriminative reconstruction pathway and makes the prior's contribution explicit and measurable rather than implicit, which is what Akshat's frozen-encoder probe is groping toward. Tu's 'Patched Denoising Diffusion Models For High-Resolution Image Synthesis' (ICLR 2024) is also directly relevant to the 2D-slice limitation Akshat's own paper lists. Second axis: Tu literally built the weakly-supervised histopathology segmentation line that Akshat's accepted MoNuSeg nucleus-segmentation paper sits in - 'Weakly Supervised Histopathology Cancer Image Segmentation and Classification' (Medical Image Analysis, 2014) and 'Multiple Clustered Instance Learning for Histopathology Cancer Image Segmentation' (CVPR 2012) - and his 'Learning Generative Models via Discriminative Approaches' (CVPR 2007) / Introspective Neural Networks line is the intellectual ancestor of using a generative objective to buy discriminative representation.
faculty.key_paper_1: Haiyang Xu*, Yu Lei*, Zeyuan Chen, Xiang Zhang, Yue Zhao, Yilin Wang, Zhuowen Tu. 'Bayesian Diffusion Models for 3D Shape Reconstruction.' CVPR 2024.
faculty.key_paper_2: Zheng Ding*, Mengqi Zhang*, Jiajun Wu, Zhuowen Tu. 'Patched Denoising Diffusion Models For High-Resolution Image Synthesis.' ICLR 2024. (Historical anchor for the medical thread: Yan Xu, Jun-Yan Zhu, Eric I-Chao Chang, Maode Lai, Zhuowen Tu, 'Weakly Supervised Histopathology Cancer Image Segmentation and Classification,' Medical Image Analysis, 2014.)
faculty.taking_students: Unstated explicitly, but the lab is very active and he directs PhD applicants to apply. Publication page (verified 2026-08-28) lists CVPR 2026 (x3), ICLR 2026, WACV 2026, NeurIPS 2025 (x2), CVPR 2025 - so the group is recruiting and producing at full rate.

faculty.notes: Confidence is Medium rather than High for two honest reasons. (1) APPOINTMENT: his primary department is COGNITIVE SCIENCE, with CSE listed as 'affiliate'. He does route PhD applicants to CSE and says they may apply to Cognitive Science simultaneously - which is a genuine second shot, since the Cognitive Science IDP has a different (earlier, ~Dec 1) deadline and is run in part by Garrison Cottrell. Confirm with CSE that an affiliate can serve as primary PhD advisor before betting the SOP on him. (2) DRIFT: his medical-imaging work (histopathology MIL, brain MRI segmentation, ROBEX skull-stripping) is 2010-2016 vintage. The 2023-2026 output is almost entirely generation, 3D reconstruction, video understanding and multimodal LLMs, much of it with Amazon/Adobe collaborators. The generative-representation overlap with Akshat's interest (B) is real and current; the medical overlap is historical. Frame the email around diffusion-as-prior, not around medical imaging.

faculty.department: Computer Science and Engineering (jointly appointed with Halicioglu Data Science Institute)
faculty.research_areas: Learning under limited supervision; the Extremely Weak Supervision (XWS) paradigm - learning a task from brief natural-language guidance instead of large annotated datasets; weakly-supervised knowledge extraction; adapting LLMs with minimal human input; bias-aware learning; scientific and enterprise text mining.
faculty.why_match: The paradigm overlap with Akshat's interest (A) is exact even though the modality is not. Shang's stated research programme is, VERBATIM from his homepage, 'scalable knowledge discovery under limited supervision ... methods that leverage semantic anchors, data redundancy, and bias-aware learning to train and adapt large language models (LLMs) with minimal human input,' centred on 'Extremely Weak Supervision (XWS), which enables task learning from brief natural-language guidance rather than large annotated datasets, similar to the task-specific guidelines provided to human annotators.' That is the same economic argument Akshat's spine result makes empirically - a teacher trained on 54 labelled images plus confidence-filtered pseudo-labels reaching 0.816 mIoU (+8.1 points over the teacher), with per-class thresholds calibratable from just 5 reference images rather than 304. Demoted to Partial rather than Close for one honest reason: Shang's supervision-efficiency work is in text/LLM space, and no specific vision or segmentation paper of his was verified in this pass, so the 'specific paper of theirs' bar is met only at the level of the research programme, not a single title.

faculty.lab: no named lab; affiliated with the UCSD AI Group (ai.ucsd.edu) and the campus learning group (learning.ucsd.edu)
faculty.research_areas: Algorithmic statistics with a focus on unsupervised and minimally supervised learning; the theory of active learning (label complexity, hierarchical sampling, importance-weighted active learning); interactive learning with feature feedback; nearest-neighbour consistency; interpretable and explainable clustering; neural algorithms inspired by the fruit-fly olfactory circuit.
faculty.why_match: Dasgupta wrote the theoretical spine of the thing Akshat did empirically. Akshat's spine study is an unusually clean measurement of label complexity: a teacher on 54 labelled images at 0.7349 mIoU, pseudo-labels filtered by per-class optimal thresholds (pseudo-label IoU 0.7437 -> 0.8529), student at 0.8162 mIoU, with MC-dropout uncertainty giving comparable but not additive gains, and thresholds transferring from a 5-image calibration set to a 304-image one. Dasgupta's 'Hierarchical sampling for active learning' (ICML 2008) and 'Coarse sample complexity bounds for active learning' (NIPS 2005) are the formal account of exactly when selective querying buys you labels, and his survey 'Two faces of active learning' (Theoretical Computer Science, 2011) is the standard framing of the stream-based vs. pool-based distinction Akshat's thresholding scheme implicitly picks a side in. His 'Framework for evaluating faithfulness of local explanations' (ICML 2022) is also methodologically adjacent to Akshat's rigorous-empiricist identity: it is a paper about whether a claimed explanation actually measures what it says.

faculty.why_match: Yu's programme is the general form of the question that falls out of Akshat's own tables: when should structure be BUILT INTO a model versus LEARNED from data? Her research thrust 'Physics-Guided Deep Learning for Spatiotemporal Dynamics' is described on her page as designing 'deep learning models that bridge the expressiveness of neural networks and the rich spatiotemporal structures from the data' - the same imposed-structure-vs-learned-structure axis that HiME sits on (chain-rule decoding makes hierarchy consistency free by construction, but Table V shows the constraint COSTS accuracy under a frozen ViT-B/16 encoder at 0.858 vs. a flat baseline's 0.888, while being free at 0.952 under full fine-tuning). Her separate thrust 'Sample Efficient Learning for Spatiotemporal Decision Making' - 'deep sequence models for Bayesian optimization ... with the goal to reduce sample complexity, provide risk assessment' - is the decision-theoretic version of Akshat's uncertainty-based pseudo-label filtering. Partial rather than Close because the domain (spatiotemporal dynamics, physical systems, time series) is not imaging and not annotation-scarcity, and because no single paper of hers was verified that directly addresses hierarchical or taxonomic constraints.

faculty.department: Halicioglu Data Science Institute (primary); Computer Science and Engineering (affiliated faculty)

faculty.research_areas: Scalable Bayesian inference for credible machine learning; uncertainty quantification in the predictions of complex models; computational and statistical guarantees for sampling algorithms (Langevin/diffusion-type dynamics); learning from time-series data and sequential decision-making.
faculty.why_match: Ma owns the formal machinery behind two of Akshat's empirical findings. (1) In the lumbar-spine study Akshat swept MC-dropout uncertainty against raw confidence thresholding as a pseudo-label filter and found MC-dropout roughly comparable (0.7910-0.7922 mIoU) and, critically, that COMBINING the two adds nothing - a negative result about the redundancy of two uncertainty estimators that Ma's programme, described verbatim on his page as 'designing Bayesian inference methods to quantify uncertainty in the predictions of complex models; understanding computational and statistical guarantees of inference algorithms,' is built to explain rather than merely observe. (2) Akshat's DDPM-pretraining work uses a denoising diffusion process as a representation learner; Ma's theoretical work on scalable sampling is the same mathematical object (Langevin-type dynamics) studied for its convergence guarantees. Partial rather than Close because Ma is a theorist working on inference algorithms, publishes no vision or medical imaging, and no specific 2023-2026 paper of his was retrieved and verified in this pass.
